indicators.note: Anything arriving in the ear is heard rather than read, so what you write down is a spelling that matches the sound.

parts.note: pain is woe, and woe said aloud is what a rider shouts to pull a horse up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pain in the ear' poses as earache. Fitting that the sound of misery turns out to be the command that halts a horse, in a puzzle this full of racing.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Stop' → WHOA: the shout that brings a horse to a standstill, so it defines stopping as an instruction rather than as a plain verb.

parts.note: a dish may be described by how it was cooked, and this is the commonest way
what a cannibal eats is man

explanation.walkthrough: Milton Friedman, the monetarist of the Chicago school, is the economist wanted; the surface carves his surname into a menu, which is the entire joke.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Economist' → FRIEDMAN: definition by example — Milton Friedman, the Chicago monetarist whose name the solver supplies from the trade named.

clue.text: Measure of alcohol in two alcoholic drinks

parts.note: the first of the two is nog, the strong ale that also flavours a Christmas eggnog
the second is gin, the spirit half of a G and T

explanation.walkthrough: One phrase has to yield both drinks, and 'two' is the only signal that the answer arrives in halves — no other word tells you where to cut.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Measure of alcohol' → NOGGIN: an old quarter-pint measure of spirits, and still the word for a small one poured for somebody.

parts.note: silver is coin, and coin in hand is cash
something no better than a copy is a mere copy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver no better than' reads as a jeweller sneering at second-rate metal. Both halves are ordinary synonyms once the sentence is broken at the right point.
explanation.definitionFit: 'fabric' → CASHMERE: the soft wool combed from Kashmir goats and woven into cloth, the region's name spelt the English way.

indicators.note: A word's origin is where it begins, and forgetting it means the opening letter never gets written down.

parts.note: a true account is a factual one
the F standing at the front is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Very' is the definition, not an intensifier: 'the very man' means the actual man, the identical one. The surface passes it off as praise for a story.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Very' → ACTUAL: the older adjectival sense heard in 'the very man' — this identical one, real rather than supposed.

clue.text: Vicious circles ending in deadlock, lose control

indicators.note: To circle something is to go the whole way round it, so the letter named next ends up enclosed.
The ending of a word is its final letter, so only the last one of deadlock is taken.

parts.note: Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols, summoned by his surname as crosswords like to do
the last letter of deadlock

explanation.walkthrough: The punk bassist hides behind an adjective: 'Vicious circles' reads as a stock phrase and is really a name with an instruction attached to it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'lose control' → SKID: once the tyres let go the car stops answering the wheel, which is precisely that loss of control.

indicators.note: One thing that passes another finishes up right alongside it — a loose join, promising only that the two pieces touch.

parts.note: cha is tea, the cup that arrives steaming
a hoot and a riot both mean something hilarious

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a ship sounding its horn in fog. Cha for tea reached English from the same Chinese word as chai, and it is standard crossword furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 → CHARIOT: 9 across is RACE, and the chariot race was the great spectacle of the Roman circus, run with two wheels and four horses.

definitions.meaning: 17 across is FLAT, which here describes the thing itself: something thin and level, cooked in a pan
9 across is RACE, and the question mark warns that this is not a flat race at a horse course but a Shrove Tuesday event with frying pans

explanation.walkthrough: Read as cross-references the clue says 'flat race', which sounds like horse racing; read literally, it asks for a flat thing that gets raced. Pancake races are run on Shrove Tuesday, runners tossing a pancake in a frying pan as they go.
explanation.definitionFit: A pancake race is the traditional British Shrove Tuesday dash, and the batter disc being carried is about as level an object as a kitchen makes.

definitions.meaning: horses and athletes run in the sense of competing over a distance
to whizz along is to travel at real speed

explanation.walkthrough: The keystone of the puzzle: a dozen other clues point at 9, each naming a different kind of one. Two ordinary senses here, a contest and sheer speed.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Run' → RACE: a run is a contest over a distance, and 'whizz' catches the other verb sense, to move so fast you tear past.

indicators.note: Things associated stand together, and that is all this join promises — it never says which piece leads, so the crossing letters settle it.

parts.note: solve 12 down first: a grey is one of them, named for the colour of its coat
to track somebody relentlessly is to hound them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Track' looks like the definition — a dog track — and is really a verb. Paul then makes you solve 12 down before this one will give up its first half.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 → GREYHOUND: 9 across is RACE, and greyhound racing, run on an oval behind a mechanical hare, is a sport in its own right.

clue.text: 9 run, ace played after finishing line

indicators.note: A tune played by ear comes out in a fresh arrangement every time, and so do these six letters.
After puts the shuffled letters behind the piece named last in the clue, so the finish stands at the front.

parts.note: the finishing line of anything is its end
six letters handed over to be resettled

explanation.walkthrough: The surface passes for a tennis report. Paul hides the join by putting the finish first, which is the last place a solver looks for the start of an answer.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 → ENDURANCE: 9 across is RACE, and an endurance race — Le Mans, the Marathon des Sables — is won by lasting rather than by pace.

clue.text: I'm thinking to enter old ruling dynasty in 9

indicators.note: To enter a place is to go inside it, so the piece holding the instruction moves in among the other's letters.

parts.note: the Han ruled China for four centuries either side of year one
the noise a person makes while thinking, written out

explanation.walkthrough: The dynasty is split after a single letter, which is where insertions get hard: the eye expects the inserted piece to land somewhere nearer the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 → HUMAN: 9 across is RACE, and the human race is the standing phrase for our species — one of the few races nobody competes in.

indicators.note: What is reported is passed on by voice, so the word wanted is the one you hear and not the one printed.

parts.note: a rough voice is a hoarse one, and that sound is spelt a second way

explanation.walkthrough: Two letters apart and a world apart: a ragged throat gives the animal that half this grid is quietly about, and the only instruction is 'Reportedly'.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 → HORSE: 9 across is RACE, and horse racing is what 'the races' means by default, from the Derby to the Grand National.

clue.text: Challenger with gun anticipated getting shot still

indicators.note: Something shot is wrecked — shot to pieces — and wrecked letters have to be rebuilt in a different order.

parts.note: a train anticipated at four is due at four
five letters handed over to be rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting shot still' sounds like a photographer at work and is two jobs at once: the shooting is the instruction, and 'still' is the word it wrecks.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Challenger with gun' → DUELLIST: the man who issues the challenge and then settles it at dawn, pistol in hand, at twenty paces.

wordplay.note: the clue is a printed gap and nothing else — what the typesetter left in front of the 9 is itself the wordplay

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is printed but the cross-reference, and the nothing is the point: the blank before 9 is a SPACE, and SPACE plus RACE is the contest to reach the moon.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 → SPACE: 9 across is RACE, and the space race was the cold-war contest between America and the Soviet Union to reach orbit and the moon.

indicators.note: On the surface that is a discount; on the letters it means one of the word's three characters, a third of them, is taken away.

parts.note: the word fee itself, all three letters of it, is the raw material
lose one of those three and FE is left, which is how chemistry writes the metal

explanation.walkthrough: Two jokes in four letters. FE is the chemical symbol, so a fee cut by a third names the metal — and 'decrease' is really de-crease, what the appliance does to a shirt.
explanation.definitionFit: 'decrease?' → IRON: read as de-crease, since taking the creases out of a shirt is ironing it, and the question mark flags the split.

parts.note: the same little word is named over and over, and how many times is what the first half of the answer counts
in cricket the on side is the leg side, so every mention supplies one leg

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is somebody droning away. 'On' is cricket's name for the leg side of the wicket, and 9 across turns three of them into a sports-day event.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 → THREE-LEGGED: 9 across is RACE, and the three-legged race is the school sports-day event run by two children with their ankles tied.

clue.text: Youngster on tour of Korea working to become firmly established

indicators.note: A youngster on tour is never in the same place twice, and letters that keep moving arrive in a new order.
Dough that is worked gets pushed about until it holds another shape, which is what happens here to the letters.

parts.note: a small child is a tot
the country contributes its own five letters, whole and unabbreviated

explanation.walkthrough: Eight letters out of two innocent words, with the definition running all the way to the full stop — 'working' belongs to the wordplay, not to the youngster.
explanation.definitionFit: 'to become firmly established' → TAKE ROOT: a seedling that takes root cannot be shifted afterwards, and the phrase carries over to ideas and habits.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dull, lifeless, without sparkle
second meaning: 9 across is RACE, and the ... is horse racing without jumps, as opposed to hurdles or steeplechase

explanation.walkthrough: In British horse racing 'the Flat' is the season and code of races run with no fences, such as the Derby.
explanation.definitionFit: A dull performance is described as lacking fizz or energy; and a flat race is the jump-free kind of horse contest.

definitions.note: 'Satirist' is a noun and the answer ends -ing, because it is a surname here rather than a participle; only the cricketing half of the clue defines the -ing word.
definitions.meaning: Henry ——, the Georgian novelist of Tom Jones and Shamela, who aimed his satire at his fellow writers
square leg and deep midwicket are places to stand in cricket, and 'perhaps' flags them as examples of the wider job

explanation.walkthrough: Two worlds in one word: a Georgian novelist, and the cricket field, where square and deep describe where a player stands rather than what shape he is.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Satirist' → FIELDING: Henry Fielding, who wrote Shamela and Tom Jones; and square or deep name positions, examples of fielding flagged by 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Snake is swimming around lake — hide!

indicators.note: A snake swimming holds no fixed shape from one moment to the next, and neither do the letters it is made of.
What goes around something closes over it, so the resettled letters finish up on both sides of the single one.

parts.note: seven letters resettled into a new order
L is the map-maker's lake, as on an atlas beside Windermere

explanation.walkthrough: The dash is the join. 'Hide!' reads as an order to conceal yourself and means a pelt, and the exclamation mark is there to keep you reading it the wrong way.
explanation.definitionFit: 'hide' → SEALSKIN: a hide is an animal's skin taken off whole, and this is that same pelt named for the creature it came from.

indicators.note: What is heard is taken in by ear, so you write the spelling that matches the sound rather than the word printed.

parts.note: harmony between people is peace, and said aloud that word is spelt a second way

explanation.walkthrough: 'Where harmony heard' poses as a concert hall, and it is the sound of calm that gives the composition. Musical surfaces are where this pair always hides.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Musical creation' → PIECE: a single composition is called a piece, the everyday word for one work rather than for a whole genre.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: 9 across is RACE, and the ... race is a children's sports-day relay of fetching vegetables one at a time
second meaning: a vegetable whose sprouting buds are called eyes

explanation.walkthrough: 'That's eyed' sounds like something being watched; it means having eyes, the buds on a tuber from which shoots grow.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuber's dormant buds are known as eyes, so it is the vegetable 'that's eyed'; and there is a traditional school sports-day event using them.

indicators.note: Cuckoo means mad, and letters sent mad will not stay in the order they were handed to you.

parts.note: nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant eater' reads as one word, herbivore, and has to be broken after the first — the standard trap when a setter starts a clue with a two-word phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Plant' → SUGAR BEET: the white-rooted crop grown across East Anglia and refined into much of Britain's sugar, so the general word covers it.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: 9 across is RACE, and in a ... race each runner hops along with both legs inside a bag
second meaning: to boot someone out is to dismiss them from their job

explanation.walkthrough: 'Boot' looks like footwear or a car's luggage space; it is the verb for firing an employee.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting the boot and getting the sack are synonymous idioms for dismissal; and the hopping bag race is a sports-day staple.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a tedious chore or person, as in 'what a ...'
second meaning: 9 across is RACE, and a ... race is a straight-line sprint between two cars from a standing start

explanation.walkthrough: Like 17 across, 'Boring' opens the clue but here it is a noun phrase, so the answer must be a thing rather than an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a tiresome task a real bore uses the same informal noun; and drag racing is the quarter-mile acceleration contest for cars.

indicators.note: A word that will not start has lost its opening letter, so you begin reading it at the second one.

parts.note: to heat something is to warm it
the opening W is the letter that never gets written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Heats' does double duty on the surface, since heats are also the qualifying rounds before a final — which is the reading Paul wants you to take.
explanation.definitionFit: 9 → ARMS: 9 across is RACE, and the arms race was the cold-war competition to stockpile more weapons than the other side had.

clue.text: Team welcomed by child able to be connected

indicators.note: To welcome somebody is to take them in, so the piece doing the welcoming closes around the other one.

parts.note: a child is a son
the team that works a boat, or a film set, is the crew

explanation.walkthrough: 'Team welcomed by child' sounds like a story from a school match. Wrapping a three-letter word around a four-letter one leaves almost nothing showing outside.
explanation.definitionFit: 'able to be connected' → SCREW-ON: a screw-on fitting is one you attach by turning it onto a thread, so it names the connectable kind.

clue.text: Partial recollection of theme, not so by George!

indicators.note: Only part of the words that follow is wanted, and that part is a run of letters lying inside them.
A recollection brings something back, and letters brought back are read the other way about.

parts.note: the letters lie consecutively across these words, running the other way

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are mild oaths: 'by George' swears by the patron saint, while the answer is the Cockney exclamation Tony Hancock turned into a catchphrase.
explanation.definitionFit: 'by George!' → STONE ME: both are exclamations of astonishment, the answer a Cockney oath heard as surprise rather than as a threat.
